extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, and readers/scholars of Darwin's correspondence
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical guidance for conducting and judging species-level natural history, taxonomy, biogeography, and variation studies (field notes, specimen comparison, use of statistics, and weighing multiple lines of evidence). Drawn from Darwin's letters discussing how to collect, describe, and reason from empirical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of trifling facts and registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Trifling observations and registers are important: 'These are the facts which make one understand the working or economy of nature.' Also endorses 'Calendar of Periodic Phenomena in Natural History' and remarks on the importance of such registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain routine registers and small, repeated observations (phenology calendars, periodic notes). Treat apparently trivial data as essential empirical input for understanding natural history and long-term patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep thorough journals and record everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin notes his difficulty in keeping a journal but emphasizes the value of recording observations and habits of observing as connected with the study of Natural History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep detailed field journals and make a deliberate habit of recording observations; lack of leisure/energy harms the ability to collect usable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minutely describe species before treating species-questions
rubrics_metrics.description: No one has a right to examine the question of species who has not 'minutely described many.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide careful, detailed morphological descriptions when publishing taxonomic work; minute, authoritative descriptions are a prerequisite for credible claims about species and their status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for variation; study domestication as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach the species question via 'variation under domestication' and collect facts on variations of domestic animals and plants; Darwin credits domestication as an instructive angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include data from domesticated forms and controlled breeding where relevant; use domestication as a model to understand how variation arises and is fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare living and extinct organisms; use biogeography and fossils
rubrics_metrics.description: Use relationships between living and extinct mammals and between continental and island faunas as evidence bearing on descent and species-change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate paleontological and geographical distribution data with living-specimen comparisons to support historical/phylogenetic inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to island affinities and geographic isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how flora and fauna of isolated islands show affinities to continental regions and whether separate islands possess distinct representative species (e.g., Galapagos, Sandwich Archipelago, St. Helena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record affinities at the island and island‑by‑island level, including possible continental source regions; prioritize sampling across islands and note representative species per island.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record habitat and elevational distribution on islands
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin observes that green leafy plants come from island summits while thin brown leafless plants come from lower arid parts, and asks that collectors bear habitats in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document precise habitat, elevation, and microhabitat for specimens (summit vs lower arid zones) because habitat often correlates with morphological and taxonomic patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study geographic range patterns at species and genus levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions whether mundane (widely distributed) genera have species with wider ranges and whether wide-ranging species imply wide-ranging genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze range size patterns explicitly—compare species-range and genus-range patterns across groups to inform conclusions about persistence, dispersal, and evolutionary history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-splitting: account for intraspecific variability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same organ is rigorously compared in many individuals, 'some slight variability' is always found; 'diagnosis of species from minute differences is always dangerous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conservative about erecting species on small differences; quantify within-species variation and use sufficiently large samples before naming distinct species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare many specimens; use rigorous comparative sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin repeatedly emphasizes that rigorous comparison of the same organ across many individuals reveals variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base taxonomic diagnoses and morphological claims on comparisons across many specimens and populations rather than single or few exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistics for life-history and population inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin stresses that without statistics one cannot conjecture duration of life, percentage of deaths to births, or fully identify when population checks fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect demographic data and apply quantitative/statistical methods (survivorship, birth/death ratios, repeat censuses) to support claims about population regulation and life-history stages where mortality acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct presence/absence and thorough surveys on small islands
rubrics_metrics.description: He asks for 'good evidence for absence of insects in small islands' and reports counting species in Keeling Atoll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic surveys to document presence/absence; absence claims require targeted, repeated sampling and should be stated cautiously unless exhaustive sampling supports them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin repeatedly notes the need for a 'grand body of facts' and combines observation, comparative anatomy, geology, and domestication evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster hypotheses with converging evidence from independent data types (field observations, collections, fossils, experiments, historical records) rather than relying on a single line of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically evaluate sources and author credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin confesses difficulty in judging the credibility of foreign authors and warns against accepting their facts uncritically; he criticizes Lamarck and Vestiges for misleading work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess primary sources for quality and reliability; cross-check doubtful claims and be cautious about adopting conclusions from authors with poor methodology or inadequate descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mechanisms (crossing, hybridization) that obscure varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: References Asa Gray's remarks on 'crossing, obliterating varieties' and the role of such processes in altering variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include consideration of hybridization, gene flow, and mating systems as processes that can merge or obscure morphological differences between populations or varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of the methodological trade-off between systematics and generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the 'frames of mind required for systematising and reasoning on large collections of facts' are opposed, and that generalizers among systematists are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and justify an approach (detailed taxonomic systematics vs broad generalization); be explicit about limitations and potential biases introduced by the chosen approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base bold inferences on strong evidence and expect criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin expresses caution about speculative conclusions, expresses fear of reproach, and asks for competent criticism of his sketch of conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting novel or controversial interpretations, document evidence transparently, acknowledge difficulties and uncertainties, invite peer critique, and avoid overclaiming beyond the data.
